passage: Last month my back tooth hurt for days, and I didn't tell anyone. I was scared the dentist would give me an injection. So I chewed on one side and said I wasn't hungry. When my sister Sarika asked to play carrom, I shouted, "Leave me alone!" and slammed the door. Ammi found me holding my cheek. "Asif, what's hurting?" I cried and told her. She wasn't angry. She hugged me and took me to the dentist the next day. The dentist explained everything first, and it wasn't as bad as I thought. I said sorry to Sarika.

qa.a: "Leave me alone!"

qa.a: Asif was scared the dentist would give an injection, so fear made hiding the pain feel safer.

qa.q: What turned things around, and what could Asif do next time?
qa.a: Telling Ammi, who hugged Asif and arranged the dentist; next time, saying something early would end the pain sooner.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt when the door slammed?
qa.a: Sarika was probably hurt and confused, not knowing the shouting came from a sore tooth.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class Three.
Chaitanya is usually chatty and busy, but for two days he has sat curled at his desk, snapping "I'm fine!" when asked anything. Today he refused to go out at break and pushed his tiffin away. At the end of break I sat beside him and said he wasn't in trouble. He whispered that his tummy had been hurting, but he hadn't told anyone because he didn't want to miss the school trip or make his mother worried. I told him telling a grown-up was the right thing, and that we would sort out the trip together. I took him to the school nurse, then phoned his mother, who came to collect him that afternoon to see their doctor. Noor (class teacher)

qa.q: What did Chaitanya push away?
qa.a: His tiffin.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya worried about when he hid his tummy ache?
qa.a: He was anxious about missing the school trip and about making his mother worried, so he kept the pain to himself.

qa.q: Which of Noor's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with him, saying he was not in trouble and reassuring him about the trip, which made it safe to talk; then the nurse and a call home the same day.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's mother feel after the call?
qa.a: She would likely be concerned but relieved that the teacher noticed and called, so he could see their doctor that day.

grounding: Illustrates a child hiding a tummy ache to avoid missing a trip or worrying a parent, with the pain showing as withdrawal and short temper.

passage: Tushar, you've been chewing on one side all week, and you snapped at your sister for nothing. Sit, let me tell you something. When I was nine, in Ambala, I had a toothache for a whole month and told nobody. I was terrified of the dentist near the bus stand; my cousin said he used a drill as big as a hammer. So I ate on one side, stopped laughing, and fought with everyone. My mother thought I had turned rude. One night she found me crying into my pillow and made me open my mouth. The next morning she held my hand in the dentist's chair the whole time. It hurt less than the month of hiding had. Your Kashish Nani learned that the hard way. So tell me, which tooth is it?

qa.q: How did Kashish's mother see her at first?
qa.a: She thought her daughter had turned rude, not knowing a hidden toothache was behind the fights.

subtype: Child hiding pain to avoid fuss [Actor]
passage: It was the week of the Class 5 sports trials, and her papa, Sumit, was working double shifts at the factory. Binita had a stomach ache that came and went, but she said nothing. If she told, she would miss the trials, and Papa already looked so tired. So she pushed away her paratha, said "I'm not hungry" in a stubborn voice, and slammed her bedroom door when Sumit asked if she was all right. That evening he found her curled on her bed, hugging her knees. "Binni, you've hardly eaten in two days. Tell me the truth." She burst into tears. "It hurts here, but I didn't want you to worry." Sumit didn't scold. He called his supervisor, took the night off, and walked her straight to the clinic down the road.

qa.q: What was happening at school that week?
qa.a: The Class 5 sports trials.

qa.q: Why did Binita hide her stomach ache?
qa.a: She was worried about missing the sports trials and anxious not to add to her tired papa's worries.

qa.q: What did Sumit do that made it safe for Binita to speak?
qa.a: He asked gently for the truth without scolding, then acted the same evening by taking the night off and going to the clinic.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel on finding out?
qa.a: Probably worried and sad that she had suffered alone to protect him.

grounding: Shows a child hiding a stomach ache to avoid missing school events or worrying a parent, with the pain leaking out as stubbornness.

subtype: Child hiding pain to avoid fuss [Actor]
passage: For three days Karthik barely spoke at dinner in their Bengaluru flat. He left his ragi mudde, said "Not hungry," and went to read in his room with the door shut. When Reena asked him to help set the table, he shouted, "Why is it always me?" which was not like him at all. Reena sat on his bed that night. "Kannu, is something hurting?" He shook his head, then covered his cheek with his hand. Slowly it came out: a back tooth throbbed whenever he chewed, and he was scared the dentist would give him an injection. "I'll be there the whole time, and you can ask the dentist to explain everything first," Reena said. She booked an appointment for the next morning.

qa.q: What did Karthik leave at dinner?
qa.a: His ragi mudde.

qa.q: What was Karthik afraid of?
qa.a: He was scared the dentist would give him an injection, so he hid the throbbing tooth and went quiet.

qa.q: What did Reena do that helped Karthik speak up?
qa.a: She noticed his changed behaviour, asked gently whether something hurt, and reassured him she would stay and he could ask questions.

qa.q: How might Reena have seen Karthik's shouting before she knew?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and hurt, since it wasn't like him, before realising pain was behind it.

grounding: Shows a child hiding a sore tooth out of fear of an injection, the pain leaking out as withdrawal and short temper.

passage:
'Shankar, why aren't you eating your payasam? It's your favourite.'
'Not hungry, Appa.'
'And why did you shout at your sister?'
'She keeps talking!'
'You didn't go to cricket either. What's going on?'
Silence. Shankar pressed his hand to his cheek.
'Is it your tooth?'
'No!' Then, very small: 'If I say, you'll take me to the dentist and he'll give an injection. And I'll miss the school trip.'
Harish sat down next to him. 'I'm glad you told me. We'll go to the dentist tomorrow, and I'll stay with you the whole time. Toothaches don't go away by hiding. I'd rather you went on the trip without pain.'
Shankar leaned into him, eyes wet.

qa.q: What did Shankar press his hand to?
qa.a: His cheek.

qa.q: What was Shankar afraid of that made him hide the pain?
qa.a: He was scared of an injection at the dentist and worried about missing the school trip.

qa.q: What did Harish say that made it easier for Shankar?
qa.a: He said he was glad Shankar told him, promised to stay with him at the dentist, and explained that hiding wouldn't make it go away.

qa.q: How might Shankar's sister have felt when he shouted?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and confused, not knowing his short temper came from a sore tooth.

grounding: A schoolchild hides a toothache for fear of injections and missing a trip, and the pain leaks out as short temper.
